blocks.text: The census measured 638 of 1006 tables and 351.3 GiB of data and index. The decision is which cost strategies and which of the 8 data-product candidates to take forward. The evidence points one way on cost: priced strategies total 1,174.4 USD a month at reference list prices, and nearly all of it comes from object stores, not from the databases.

Database reclaim is only 15.2 GiB, 4.3% of bytes. Data quality and personal-data exposure are the larger concerns: 23.0% of rows are degraded and 71.8% of sampled rows carry markers. We recommend verifying the two object-store strategies, deferring database housekeeping, and releasing no product externally until rights are declared and bound. All savings are estimates, not realised returns.
The estate holds 351.3 GiB of data and index. The largest databases hold 350.3 GiB of it, which is 99.7%, and one staging database accounts for nearly all of that.
For the owner this means database savings are bounded by a very small footprint. Effort spread across the many small databases will move the total very little.

blocks.text: Exact duplicate rows are 1.5% of rows. Degraded rows are 23.0%, rows with empty required-looking fields are 81.7%, and 71.8% of sampled rows carry personal-data markers. Bytes not written for over a year are 15.4% of the total.

Duplication is therefore a minor cost lever. The larger issues are completeness and personal-data exposure, and they decide which data products are worth building. The empty-field label is a heuristic, and the marker ratio comes from a sample, so both should be read as indicative.

sections.heading: Almost all addressable bytes are in object and file stores

blocks.text: Coverage is partial: 638 of 1006 tables were measured. Of 351.3 GiB held, 350.3 GiB is in the largest databases. Reclaimable bytes before pricing are 15.2 GiB, 4.3% of database bytes.
Dead columns are 13.0% of measured columns. That supports a tidying exercise but does not by itself reduce cost.

sections.heading: Scope and scale of the database estate

blocks.text: Exact duplicates (1.5%) are small beside degraded rows (23.0%), empty required-looking fields (81.7%) and personal-data markers (71.8%). Together these set the cleansing and de-identification effort that any data product must absorb.
These ratios come from complete passes where the table allowed and stratified samples elsewhere, so they carry sampling uncertainty.
Personal-data markers were checked on 1.0m million sampled rows. Bytes not written for over a year are 15.4% of the total, there are 71 duplicate table pairs, and 368 of 1006 tables are empty.

None of these is a large saving on its own. Duplicate pairs may be deliberate staging or backup copies, and an empty table may be freshly truncated, so each needs an owner's confirmation before action.

Archive-class storage for old buckets would save 986.5 USD a month across 42,891.0 GiB. Reconciling duplicate objects would save 180.3 USD across 7,839.5 GiB. Moving old tables to cold storage would save 5.9 USD across 54.1 GiB.

All three are estimates at reference list prices. The first depends on read frequency, which was not measured, and on retrieval fees. The second depends on candidates matching on listing details and size, not content, and must be confirmed before any deletion.

blocks.text: Start with the two object-store strategies, because they carry nearly all of the 1,174.4 USD monthly total. Check read frequency before archiving, and confirm duplicates by content hash before deleting. Neither step needs new rights.

Defer database housekeeping, where reclaim is 15.2 GiB. Release no data product externally: rights are declared, not measured, and markers appear in 71.8% of sampled rows. Grant access to artists_app and rerun the census on sampled tables so later decisions rest on complete passes.

sections.heading: What to do first, and why

blocks.text: Four gaps limit the evidence. Sampled ratios are estimates until a complete pass is run. Rights, licences and semantic similarity are unmeasured, so the 8 candidates are dimensional readiness only. The artists_app connection could not be read until a MySQL grant is made. File-share duplication is unknown, and some buckets were unreachable.
Prices are reference list prices, not the owner's invoice. Savings therefore indicate scale and ordering, and should not be booked as returns.
